newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW-Australian labour force data.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-INSTANT VIEW-Australian labour force data.

text.p: Australian employment rose by 4,500 in December and the unemployment rate was 8.6 percent, the Australian Bureau of Statistics reported.
Economists' median forecast had been for a rise in December employment of 5,000 and an unemployment rate of 8.6 percent.

Forecasts for employment ranged from a fall of 25,000 to a rise of 15,000, while unemployment forecasts ranged from 8.3 to 8.7 percent. The following is a selection of economists' initial reation to the data.
HANS KUNNEN, CHIEF ECONOMIST, COLONIAL STATE BANK:

"Given that we have at least 15,000 people joining the workforce each month, what they say to us is that the unemployment rate is going to rise over time, and they do reflect the weakness that we have seen in the December quarter. They will certainly give the markets some encouragement (about another interest rate cut). The Reserve Bank would have been aware of the weakness in the economy, that's why they eased rates in December and these are December figures."
CHRIS CATON, CHIEF ECONOMIST, BANKERS TRUST:

"They're remarkably close to expectations and if anything they may dampen the over-hyping that was going on beforehand that if we got a bad number today there'd be even more talk about an almost immediate cut in rates. These are not spectacularly good figures you understand, but they're certainly not bad enough to mandate that kind of hyperbole."
JOHN PETERS, MARKET ECONOMIST, WESTPAC BANKING CORP:

"(The data) bolsters the case for a rate cut in early 1997. The 4,500 puts the annual growth rate at 0.8 percent, which is still too feeble a rate to bring about a sustainable reduction in the unemployment rate. We think the chances are very good for a rate cut in the next couple of months."
MICHAEL BLYTHE, SENIOR ECONOMIST, COMMONWEALTH BANK:

"It is a volatile series and it is interesting to note that if you average the last three months you get an average employment growth of 18,000 per month. That's pretty well consistent with what the Australian Bureau of Statistics measure of job vacancies is suggesting employment should be, around 15,000 to 20,000 per month on average. We are more or less right in the middle of that range. I wouldn't read too much into the 4,500 figure for today."
STEPHEN ROBERTS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, UBS AUSTRALIA:

"It's neutralish, but I suppose it's not as weak as perhaps people might have thought because when you put it all together you've had three months now which have generated 55,000 jobs. In a way, the softest part of the employment market was much earlier in the year (1996) and if anything things actually firmed a bit running through the second half. Obviously we need more than 4,500 (jobs) a month to get the unemployment rate to come down, but the risk is more towards that as you get some pick up in economic activity through 1997."

"At face value, the numbers are pretty much in line with expectations. We've got employment growth chugging along at about 8,000 to 10,000 a month, which is enough to prevent an upward drift in unemployment. But with this announcement about the new survey, I think it's a reasonably large number per month (6,000 to 9,000). It's (the labour market) clearly then a little stronger than we thought."

"We're seeing a very weak labour market with no trend improvement in unemployment so far. This number will keep the heat on the Reserve Bank in terms of the unemployment problem the economy's got. Having eased already three times in the space of less than six months, it strikes me that it's only a 50-50 chance that we'll see an easing at the February board meeting and probably slightly better than 50 at the March meeting."
